title: Ingesting live market data from Databento into QuestDB
summary: Stream every US equity quote and trade from Databento into QuestDB with one config file, query it with SQL, and keep every row through restarts and failover.
body_markdown:
QuestDB is the open-source time-series database for demanding workloads—from trading floors to mission control. It delivers ultra-low latency, high ingestion throughput, and a multi-tier storage engine. Native support for Parquet and SQL keeps your data portable, AI-ready—no vendor lock-in.


---


In a[previous post](https://questdb.com/blog/ingesting-live-market-data-data-bento/) we ingested Databento market data into QuestDB with Python code and visualized it in Grafana. On QuestDB open source that's still the way to do it, and the[Databento with Python](https://questdb.com/docs/integrations/other/databento/) guide covers it. On QuestDB Enterprise there's now a better option: a[Databento connector](https://questdb.com/docs/connect/connectors/databento/) that replaces that code with a config file and keeps your history complete across restarts and failover, with dashboards that run directly in the QuestDB Web Console.


Below, we stream every US equity quote and trade from Databento's` EQUS.MINI` dataset into QuestDB, query it with SQL, and then stop both the connector and the database mid-stream to check that nothing goes missing. Everything comes from real runs on October 16th, 2026, and the full example is in our[blog-examples repository](https://github.com/questdb/blog-examples/tree/main/2026-10-databento-orderbook-ingestion) .


It's a long post, so here's what's in it:


- Databento and the EQUS.MINI dataset : what the data is, and what you need to follow along
- Configuring andrunning the Databento connector : one config file and one long-running process
- What the connector writes to QuestDB : the table schema and the order book arrays
- Querying Databento quotes and trades with SQL :` LATEST ON` ,` SAMPLE BY` ,` ASOF JOIN` , and a live Web Console dashboard
- Spreads, microbursts and nanosecond timestamps : what three pre-market minutes contain
- Restarting the connector without a gap : Databento intraday replay, and handling duplicates
- High availability : QuestDB outages, upgrades, and failover to a replica
- Retention and cold storage : storage policies that move history to Parquet in object storage


---


## Databento and the EQUS.MINI dataset


[Databento](https://databento.com/) is a market data provider. It takes direct feeds from exchanges and trading venues, normalizes them into one format, and serves them live or historically through a single API. Each source is a dataset, such as CME Globex futures (` GLBX.MDP3` ), and each dataset comes in schemas of increasing detail: trades, top of book (` mbp-1` ), ten levels of depth (` mbp-10` ), or every individual order (` mbo` ).


This post uses[Databento US Equities Mini](https://databento.com/docs/venues-and-datasets/equs-mini) , dataset ID` EQUS.MINI` . It blends direct feeds from several US exchanges and alternative trading systems into a single composite best bid and offer per stock, along with the trades. It's top of book only, with no depth beyond the best level, but one subscription covers the whole US equities market, and it's Databento's lowest-cost real-time equities feed. We subscribe to two of its schemas:` mbp-1` , which carries every change to the best bid and offer plus trade events, and` trades` , which carries trades only.


Warning


To follow along you need QuestDB Enterprise 4.0.0 or later, and a Databento account with a paid subscription that includes live data. As of writing, Databento doesn't offer usage-based live access to its US equities data, and the free credits you get on sign-up only apply to historical data. See[Databento pricing](https://databento.com/pricing) for the current plans.


Without live access, you can still use the sign-up credits with the connector's[Historical mode](https://questdb.com/docs/connect/connectors/databento/#historical-backfills) to load a past window into the same tables and run the queries. The restart experiments need a live session.


---


## Configuring the Databento connector


The connector reads a single config file,` connector.toml` in the example. It names the dataset and, for each Databento schema, the symbols and the QuestDB table to write to:` mbp-1` goes to` equs_orderbook` and` trades` to` equs_trades` , both for` ALL_SYMBOLS` . It also sets a state directory for checkpoints and turns on` replay_dedup` , both covered in the restart sections below. Credentials come from environment variables, not the file. The connector writes with[QWP](https://questdb.com/blog/questdb-qwp-binary-wire-protocol/) , QuestDB's binary protocol over WebSocket.


---


## Running the Databento connector against live US equities


You need QuestDB Enterprise 4.0.0 or later, a Databento API key with Live access to` EQUS.MINI` , and the` databento-questdb` binary, which you get through your QuestDB Enterprise contact. The[connector docs](https://questdb.com/docs/connect/connectors/databento/#1-install-the-connector) cover installing it.


Set your credentials, pointing` QDB_CLIENT_CONF` at your QuestDB, and start the connector:


```text
export DATABENTO_API_KEY='db-your-key-here'   export QDB_CLIENT_CONF='ws::addr=localhost:9000;token=<your-token>;'   databento-questdb --config connector.toml
```


The token belongs to a[service account](https://questdb.com/docs/connect/connectors/databento/#questdb-authentication-and-tls) with` HTTP` and` CREATE TABLE` grants, so the connector's access doesn't depend on any person's permissions.


The connector is a long-running process. In production you'd run it under systemd, Docker or Kubernetes and leave it alone. For this example, it streams until you press Ctrl+C.` ALL_SYMBOLS` is a heavy stream during market hours, so stop it once you have enough data. On Ctrl+C or` SIGTERM` it stops reading, drains the rows in flight, waits for QuestDB to acknowledge them, and saves its checkpoint.


The connector logs a progress line every 60 seconds by default, and every 30 in the example. This one is from our first run:


```text
INFO databento_questdb: progress connector=equs-mini status=Running received=34732 published=34727 confirmed=34727 confirmation_lag=mbp-1=0.1s,trades=2.0s
```


` received` counts records from Databento,` published` counts rows written to QuestDB, and` confirmed` counts rows QuestDB has acknowledged. The checkpoint only moves with` confirmed` , so a restart never skips data that was received but not yet stored.


That run was US pre-market, 07:49 to 07:53 in New York, and three minutes produced about 37,000 top-of-book updates across a few hundred symbols, around 200 a second. At the 10:00 open, the dashboard further down shows the same feed at 20,000 to 65,000 book updates a second, two orders of magnitude more.


---


## What the connector writes to QuestDB: nanosecond tables and order book arrays


There's no DDL step. The connector creates both tables on first write, partitioned by day, with WAL enabled, nanosecond timestamps, and Databento's receive time` ts_recv` as the[designated timestamp](https://questdb.com/docs/concepts/designated-timestamp/) . This is the table it created for` mbp-1` :


equs_orderbook, as created by the connector


```text
CREATE TABLE 'equs_orderbook' (       dataset SYMBOL,       symbol SYMBOL,       publisher_id INT,       instrument_id LONG,       ts_event TIMESTAMP_NS,       price DOUBLE,       size LONG,       action SYMBOL,       side SYMBOL,       flags SHORT,       depth SHORT,       ts_recv TIMESTAMP_NS,       ts_in_delta LONG,       sequence LONG,       bids DOUBLE[][],       asks DOUBLE[][],       bid_ct DOUBLE[],       ask_ct DOUBLE[]   ) timestamp(ts_recv) PARTITION BY DAY;
```


Every row carries` dataset` ,` publisher_id` ,` instrument_id` and the resolved` symbol` , so the instrument-ID dictionary from the old script is gone. The other change is how the book is stored. Bids and asks are[two-dimensional arrays](https://questdb.com/docs/query/datatypes/array/) of shape` \[2, N\]` , best level first: row 1 holds prices and row 2 sizes.` bids\[1\]\[1\]` is the best bid and` bids\[2\]\[1\]` its size. For` mbp-1` ,` N` is 1. Subscribe to a deeper schema such as` mbp-10` and the same columns hold ten levels, so none of the queries below change shape.


An empty side of the book is` NULL` . In our pre-market sample 27% of book updates had an empty bid or ask, which is normal for thinly traded names before the open.


The` mbp-1` table also contains trade events, with` action = 'T'` , next to adds (` A` ), cancels (` C` ) and modifies (` M` ). The separate` trades` subscription is there for convenience: smaller scans when you only want prints.


If you want different partitioning, symbol capacity or retention, create the table yourself before starting the connector. It uses an existing compatible table as it is.


---


## Querying Databento quotes and trades with SQL


All the queries are in` sql/queries.sql` in the example, and` python3 run_sql.py sql/queries.sql <name>` runs any of them over the REST API. They also run as they are in the Web Console. The results below are from the pre-market run.


### Latest top of book per symbol with LATEST ON


[LATEST ON](https://questdb.com/docs/query/sql/latest-on/) returns the most recent row per symbol without a self-join or a window function:


Latest top of book per symbol


```text
SELECT ts_recv, symbol,          bids[1][1] AS bid_px, bids[2][1] AS bid_sz,          asks[1][1] AS ask_px, asks[2][1] AS ask_sz   FROM equs_orderbook   WHERE symbol IN ('AAPL', 'MSFT', 'NVDA', 'TSLA', 'SPY', 'QQQ')   LATEST ON ts_recv PARTITION BY symbol;
```


ts_recv symbol bid_px bid_sz ask_px ask_sz


2026-10-16T11:50:02.171043697Z TSLA 373.5 92 376.77 60


2026-10-16T11:52:44.511284405Z SPY 772.33 146 772.44 100


2026-10-16T11:52:44.544151599Z QQQ 726.19 200 726.27 200


Three of the six symbols are missing. AAPL, MSFT and NVDA didn't update their quotes once in those three pre-market minutes, and` LATEST ON` only returns symbols that have data. During regular hours all six show up.


### OHLC bars from raw trades with SAMPLE BY


[SAMPLE BY](https://questdb.com/docs/query/sql/sample-by/) buckets rows by time, which turns raw trades into one-minute bars:


One-minute OHLCV bars from raw trades


```text
SELECT ts_recv, symbol,          first(price) AS open, max(price) AS high,          min(price) AS low, last(price) AS close,          sum(size) AS volume, count() AS trades   FROM equs_trades   SAMPLE BY 1m   ORDER BY trades DESC   LIMIT 10;
```


To keep bars like these current as trades arrive, without recomputing them on every read, put the query in a[materialized view](https://questdb.com/blog/how-to-create-a-materialized-view/) .


### Each trade against the prevailing quote with ASOF JOIN


[ASOF JOIN](https://questdb.com/docs/query/sql/asof-join/) matches each trade with the latest quote for the same symbol at or before the trade's timestamp:


Where each trade printed relative to the quote


```text
SELECT t.ts_recv, t.symbol, t.price, t.size,          q.bids[1][1] AS bid_px, q.asks[1][1] AS ask_px,          CASE              WHEN q.bids[1][1] = NULL OR q.asks[1][1] = NULL                  THEN 'no two-sided quote'              WHEN t.price >= q.asks[1][1] THEN 'at or above ask'              WHEN t.price <= q.bids[1][1] THEN 'at or below bid'              ELSE 'inside spread'          END AS trade_location   FROM equs_trades t   ASOF JOIN equs_orderbook q ON (symbol)   LIMIT -10;
```


ts_recv symbol price size bid_px ask_px trade_location


...


2026-10-16T11:52:33.813857415Z NBIS 182.75 60 182 186 inside spread


2026-10-16T11:52:35.558939201Z ZTG 0.7606 500 0.7467 0.7606 at or above ask


2026-10-16T11:52:39.022430815Z TCRT 2.8 25 2.79 2.8 at or above ask


2026-10-16T11:52:43.827566173Z RUBI 0.436 28 0.436 0.5231 at or below bid


The` = NULL` comparison is deliberate: QuestDB doesn't accept` IS NULL` on an array element. Aggregating the same join over every trade shows what thin early trading looks like:


trade_location trades shares


no two-sided quote 62 13009


inside spread 52 9233


at or below bid 38 2066


at or above ask 11 1657


62 of 163 pre-market trades printed while that symbol's book was one-sided. Keep only trades and you'd never know.


For transaction cost analysis, note that the matched quote occasionally already reflects the trade itself, because both carry the same nanosecond. An` LT JOIN` avoids that; the[time-series joins guide](https://questdb.com/blog/questdb-time-series-joins-guide/) covers the difference, and our[TCA post](https://questdb.com/blog/transaction-cost-analysis-questdb-polars/) adds markouts with` HORIZON JOIN` .


### A live dashboard in the Web Console, no Grafana needed


Grafana still works with QuestDB, but you don't need it for this. The Web Console has[notebooks that work as live dashboards](https://questdb.com/docs/getting-started/web-console/notebooks/live-dashboards/) , with charts, auto-refresh and variables. The example ships one as` questdb-databento-dashboard.json` . Open the menu at the right end of the Web Console tab bar, choose **Import tabs** , and it opens as a new notebook in a 2x2 grid.


It has four cells:


- **Trades: OHLC (5s) and Volume.** Candles from raw trades with` SAMPLE BY 5s` , volume on a second axis.
- **Top of Book: Bid, Ask and Spread (1s).** Best bid and ask read straight from the arrays, with the spread in basis points from the native` spread()` and` mid()` functions.
- **Most Active Symbols (last 60s).** The ten symbols with the most quote updates, their latest quote from` LATEST ON` , spread, trades and last price.
- **Feed Activity: Updates and Trades per Second.** The whole feed, all symbols.


Databento EQUS.MINI in the QuestDB Web Console, captured at the 10:00 New York open


Two notebook variables parameterize it:` @symbol` (` 'NVDA'` by default) and` @asof` (` now()` ). Each cell anchors its window to the newest data up to` @asof` , so the dashboard still renders after the connector stops, and setting` @asof` to an earlier instant replays that window.


At the open, NVDA's spread mostly sat between 1 and 3 basis points with spikes past 12, QQQ and IWM quoted under 1, and TQQQ, the busiest quote stream, updated 35,536 times in a single minute.


---


## Spreads, microbursts and nanosecond timestamps in three pre-market minutes


A quiet session still has plenty in it once every update is stored. These all run over the same pre-market sample: 37,321 book updates across 393 symbols.


### Bid-ask spread percentiles per symbol


QuestDB has native` spread()` and` mid()` functions, which shorten the basis point formula:


Spread distribution for the most quoted symbols


```text
SELECT symbol,          min(spread(bids[1][1], asks[1][1])              / mid(bids[1][1], asks[1][1]) * 10000) AS min_bps,          approx_percentile(spread(bids[1][1], asks[1][1])              / mid(bids[1][1], asks[1][1]) * 10000, 0.5, 3) AS p50_bps,          max(spread(bids[1][1], asks[1][1])              / mid(bids[1][1], asks[1][1]) * 10000) AS max_bps,          count() AS updates   FROM equs_orderbook   WHERE bids[1][1] > 0 AND asks[1][1] > 0   ORDER BY updates DESC   LIMIT 8;
```


symbol min_bps p50_bps max_bps updates


QQQ 0.826 1.239 3.029 4134


SQQQ 2.742 2.744 5.495 2064


TQQQ 2.726 4.092 230.629 1553


QLD 2.175 3.266 61.069 1516


SLV 3.834 3.834 9.585 1349


IVV 0.644 1.160 2.578 1308


SPY 0.647 1.036 7.251 1217


USO 1.901 3.171 334.331 1035


The most actively quoted names before the open are all ETFs, and SPY, IVV and QQQ sit around a basis point at the median. The maximums are another story: TQQQ and USO each quoted more than 200 basis points wide at some point, and you only see that if you kept every update.


One detail if you reuse the query:` approx_percentile` needs the precision argument,` 3` here. With the default, SQQQ's median came out below its minimum.


### Nanosecond timestamps: event time vs receive time


Each Databento record carries two timestamps,` ts_event` and` ts_recv` , and the connector stores both at nanosecond precision:


Gap between the event and receive timestamps


```text
SELECT approx_percentile((ts_recv - ts_event) / 1000.0, 0.5, 3) AS p50_us,          approx_percentile((ts_recv - ts_event) / 1000.0, 0.99, 3) AS p99_us,          approx_percentile((ts_recv - ts_event) / 1000.0, 0.999, 3) AS p999_us,          max((ts_recv - ts_event) / 1000.0) AS max_us,          count() AS updates   FROM equs_orderbook   WHERE ts_recv >= ts_event;
```


p50_us p99_us p999_us max_us updates


18.383 25.539 33.867 42.207 37321


The gap is about 18 microseconds at the median and 42 at the worst. Round those timestamps to microseconds and much of that distribution turns into noise.


### Finding microbursts with SAMPLE BY


Per-second update rates


```text
SELECT max(n) AS peak_per_second, avg(n) AS avg_per_second,          approx_percentile(n, 0.99, 3) AS p99_per_second,          count() AS seconds   FROM (SELECT ts_recv, count() AS n FROM equs_orderbook SAMPLE BY 1s);
```


peak_per_second avg_per_second p99_per_second seconds


1089 200.651 865 186


The average was 200 updates a second and the busiest second carried more than five times that.` SAMPLE BY` goes down to milliseconds with` 1T` , so we can look inside that second:


The busiest single milliseconds


```text
SELECT ts_recv, count() AS updates, count_distinct(symbol) AS symbols   FROM equs_orderbook   SAMPLE BY 1T   ORDER BY updates DESC   LIMIT 5;
```


ts_recv updates symbols


2026-10-16T11:51:30.682000000Z 350 178


2026-10-16T11:51:35.228000000Z 185 77


2026-10-16T11:51:30.683000000Z 137 55


2026-10-16T11:51:40.179000000Z 131 52


2026-10-16T11:51:40.178000000Z 78 51


A single millisecond at 11:51:30.682 carried 350 updates across 178 symbols. Breaking those two milliseconds down by action and side:


What happened in the busiest two milliseconds


```text
SELECT action, side, count() AS updates,          count_distinct(symbol) AS symbols,          min(ts_event), max(ts_event)   FROM equs_orderbook   WHERE ts_recv BETWEEN '2026-10-16T11:51:30.682Z'                     AND '2026-10-16T11:51:30.684Z';
```


action side updates symbols min(ts_event) max(ts_event)


C B 161 100 2026-10-16T11:51:30.682328257Z 2026-10-16T11:51:30.683970175Z


C A 260 160 2026-10-16T11:51:30.682330164Z 2026-10-16T11:51:30.683776869Z


A A 37 25 2026-10-16T11:51:30.682351205Z 2026-10-16T11:51:30.683965004Z


A B 28 18 2026-10-16T11:51:30.682363467Z 2026-10-16T11:51:30.683971474Z


T A 1 1 2026-10-16T11:51:30.682512172Z 2026-10-16T11:51:30.682512172Z


421 cancels on both sides of the book, across well over a hundred symbols, in 1.7 milliseconds, followed by a handful of new quotes. It looks like a liquidity provider pulling quotes across many names at once, though the data can't say who. It's also why ingestion has to be sized for the peak, not the average.


---


## Restarting the connector without a gap: Databento intraday replay


The first question I got when I showed this internally was: if the connector is down for five minutes, how do you get those five minutes back?


The connector saves the position of the last record QuestDB acknowledged into` state_dir` , once a second by default and again on shutdown. When it starts with the same state directory, it asks Databento's Live gateway to replay from just before that point using[intraday replay](https://databento.com/docs/api-reference-live/basics/intraday-replay) , then carries on with live data. Databento generally keeps 24 hours of replay.


We stopped the connector at 11:51:39 UTC and started it again at 11:51:44. It logged a recovery start for each schema, and Databento reported the replay complete about a second later. Counting book updates in 30-second buckets across the stop and restart:


Arrival timeline across a restart


```text
SELECT ts_recv, count() AS book_updates   FROM equs_orderbook   SAMPLE BY 30s;
```


ts_recv book_updates


2026-10-16T11:49:30.000000000Z 3556


2026-10-16T11:50:00.000000000Z 5810


2026-10-16T11:50:30.000000000Z 5169


2026-10-16T11:51:00.000000000Z 6569


2026-10-16T11:51:30.000000000Z 7964


2026-10-16T11:52:00.000000000Z 4725


2026-10-16T11:52:30.000000000Z 3528


The 11:51:30 bucket contains the outage and is the fullest in the run. An earlier test with about 38 seconds of downtime gave the same result. I haven't yet tested a five-minute stop, but the mechanism doesn't depend on the length of the outage as long as it fits inside Databento's replay window.


For an outage longer than the replay window, the connector has a[Historical mode](https://questdb.com/docs/connect/connectors/databento/#historical-backfills) that backfills a bounded range into the same tables. Databento bills Historical data separately.


### Duplicates, replay_dedup, and why not DEDUP keys


Delivery is at least once. The replay deliberately starts a few seconds before the checkpoint, 5 by default, to cover records that were in flight, so without filtering those seconds are written twice. We measured both ways:


Run Rows in the replay overlap Distinct rows Duplicates


` replay_dedup = false` 2,367 1,224 1,143


` replay_dedup = true` n/a n/a 0


` replay_dedup = true` drops those replayed records inside the connector, before they reach QuestDB. Along with each checkpoint, the connector saves, for every instrument, the timestamp of the last record it wrote and how many records it wrote at exactly that timestamp. During the replay it skips every record for that instrument with an earlier timestamp, skips the first N records at the saved timestamp, and writes everything after that, following Databento's guidance on[recovering after a disconnection](https://databento.com/docs/api-reference-live/basics/recovering-after-a-disconnection) . It counts records instead of comparing them, so two genuine records that happen to be identical are both kept.


In our run it skipped about 2,150 replayed records, and the only identical rows left in either table were single genuine prints that match in every field. The filter assumes that` ts_event` never goes backwards for a given instrument, and that records sharing a timestamp always arrive in the same order. We checked the first across 33,263` EQUS.MINI` book updates and it never went backwards.


The obvious alternative is QuestDB's own[DEDUP UPSERT KEYS](https://questdb.com/docs/concepts/deduplication/) , which makes repeated writes idempotent. It needs a key that's unique per real record, and` EQUS.MINI` doesn't have one.` sequence` is always 0 in this dataset, and` (ts_recv, instrument_id)` isn't unique: 233 of 34,409 book rows and 14 of 324 trades shared that pair with another genuine record. Even a key over every scalar column left four identical genuine rows per table. A` DEDUP` key here would collapse those genuine twins into one row and silently drop real data. The connector's count-based filter doesn't have that problem, so for this dataset it's the right place to remove replay duplicates. On datasets that publish venue sequence numbers, a` DEDUP` key that includes` sequence` becomes an option.


---


## High availability: keeping the Databento feed when QuestDB goes away


QuestDB can also become unreachable while the connector keeps running: a planned stop such as an upgrade, a network hiccup, or a primary that fails for good. The connector treats that as a temporary condition, not a failure. It keeps the Databento session open and keeps receiving. Rows QuestDB hasn't acknowledged stay in memory, in the QuestDB client's[store-and-forward](https://questdb.com/docs/connect/wire-protocols/qwp-client-behavior/) buffer and in the connector's own queue, and the writer retries until QuestDB is back, then sends everything. Because every row carries Databento's` ts_recv` as its designated timestamp, rows that arrive late are still stored at the moment they happened, not at the moment QuestDB came back.


We stopped QuestDB with` docker stop` for 2 minutes and 12 seconds in the middle of a run. The connector's progress log, times in UTC:


```text
12:00:06 progress status=Running received=11433 published=11433 confirmed=11433 unconfirmed_batches=0 retries=0      (QuestDB stopped at 12:00:26)   12:00:36 progress status=Running received=20856 published=18158 confirmed=17518 confirmation_lag=mbp-1=10.2s unconfirmed_batches=64 retries=0   12:01:36 progress status=Running received=38510 published=18158 confirmed=17518 confirmation_lag=mbp-1=70.2s unconfirmed_batches=64 retries=0   12:02:36 progress status=Running received=56099 published=18158 confirmed=17518 confirmation_lag=mbp-1=130.3s unconfirmed_batches=64 retries=0      (QuestDB started at 12:02:38)   12:03:06 progress status=Running received=63144 published=63144 confirmed=63144 confirmation_lag=mbp-1=0.1s unconfirmed_batches=0 retries=0
```


` status=Running` holds throughout: the task never failed and the process never restarted.` received` keeps climbing while` published` and` confirmed` stand still, which is the connector holding the live feed in memory.` retries=0` means the Databento session never dropped, so no replay was needed. Within 30 seconds of QuestDB coming back,` confirmed` had caught up with` received` and the lag was back to 0.1 seconds.


In QuestDB, the outage is fully populated, each row at its original Databento timestamp:


ts_recv book_updates QuestDB


2026-10-16T12:00:00.000000000Z 10698 up


2026-10-16T12:00:30.000000000Z 10288 down from 12:00:26


2026-10-16T12:01:00.000000000Z 7804 down


2026-10-16T12:01:30.000000000Z 8764 down


2026-10-16T12:02:00.000000000Z 8276 down


2026-10-16T12:02:30.000000000Z 6966 back at 12:02:38


2026-10-16T12:03:00.000000000Z 7737 up


The duplicate check afterwards found nothing beyond the single genuine identical print per table that shows up in every run.


### Failover to a new primary with replication


With replication, the same mechanism covers losing the primary for good. Give the connector every node of the cluster in` QDB_CLIENT_CONF` :


```text
export QDB_CLIENT_CONF='wss::addr=node-a:9000,node-b:9000;token=<your-token>;target=primary;request_durable_ack=on;'
```


` target=primary` sends the connector's table-creation queries to the primary. Changing the endpoints or the acknowledgement level needs a new` state_dir` , so set this up before the first run.


While the primary is unreachable, the client cycles through the addresses. Replicas refuse writes, so it keeps buffering until you, or a watchdog of your own,[promote a replica](https://questdb.com/blog/questdb-enterprise-4-0-release/#when-the-primary-goes-away-failover-without-a-restart) to primary, and then sends everything to the new primary.` request_durable_ack=on` makes the connector count rows as confirmed only once they're durably uploaded to object storage, not when the old primary first accepted them, so rows it already considered safe aren't lost with that node.


### Limits of buffering during a QuestDB outage


The buffer is memory, so it's bounded. Our test ran before the open at about 260 records a second. At the open the same subscription runs at tens of thousands a second, and the buffers fill in a fraction of the time. When they do, the connector pauses reading from Databento rather than dropping data or failing.


While reads are paused, Databento queues the records instead of skipping ahead, and the connector logs a` SlowReaderWarning` . Only a backlog that outlives Databento's replay window fails the task, and then a[Historical backfill](https://questdb.com/docs/connect/connectors/databento/#replay-availability) fills the gap. We haven't tested that path yet, on regular hours data with a long QuestDB outage, so treat it as designed rather than measured.


For a planned QuestDB stop, keep the connector running rather than restarting both. If QuestDB is down when the connector starts, its first connection fails by default.

## Retention and cold storage for market data in QuestDB


Three pre-market minutes say nothing about the size of a trading day, so I won't put a storage number on this.


Partitioning by day, the connector's default, means retention works on whole days. A[storage policy](https://questdb.com/docs/concepts/storage-policy/) decides how long each partition stays on local disk and can send it to[cold storage](https://questdb.com/docs/concepts/cold-storage/) : S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage, or a filesystem store such as an NFS mount:


Copy order book history to cold storage daily


```text
ALTER TABLE equs_orderbook SET STORAGE POLICY(       TO REMOTE 1 DAY,       DROP LOCAL 7 DAYS   );
```


` TO REMOTE 1 DAY` uploads each daily partition as Parquet once all of it is more than a day old, so Monday's order book is in your data lake shortly after midnight on Wednesday, ready for any tool that reads Parquet. QuestDB still serves queries from the local copy until` DROP LOCAL 7 DAYS` removes it, and after that the same SQL reads the Parquet files in cold storage, fetching only the row groups and columns a query needs.


` DROP LOCAL` also seals a partition read-only, and later writes to it are skipped. Seven days is well beyond Databento's 24-hour replay window, but keep it longer than any Historical backfill or correction you might run.

## Wrapping up: Databento market data in QuestDB


The pipeline is one config file. The connector creates the tables and the order book arrays,` LATEST ON` ,` SAMPLE BY` and` ASOF JOIN` work on nanosecond data from the first minute, and the dashboard runs in the Web Console. A connector restart backfills itself from Databento's replay, and a QuestDB outage, or a failover to a replica, loses nothing and keeps the original timestamps.


Getting data in is half of it. Research and replay also need the data back out, and in a future post we'll look at reading these tables from QuestDB as Arrow.


The[example code](https://github.com/questdb/blog-examples/tree/main/2026-10-databento-orderbook-ingestion) has everything above, and the[connector docs](https://questdb.com/docs/connect/connectors/databento/) cover the configuration options this post skipped: authentication and TLS, multiple datasets in one process, metrics, Historical backfills, and materialized and live views over the connector's tables.
